_comment: Content for the per-test pages of the V&V site. One entry per test page. Definitions and expected results are paraphrased from the standards (no verbatim copies, no reproduced figures); 'source' gives clause, page and figure so readers can check the original. 'coverage' joins to standards/coverage.json by standard id plus row id, and by row name where a row id repeats (NIST Verif.2.2 up/down). 'scenario_files' lists the canonical scenario zips the test runs (decision D18; empty when the scenario is built in code or not implemented). 'deviations' lists how the implementation differs from the standard. Pages are generated by scripts/gen_vv_site.py.

tests.title: Maintaining a set walking speed in a corridor
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 1, para. 3, p. 9
tests.definition: One person walks along a corridor 2 m wide and 40 m long. The person's set walking speed is 1 m/s.
tests.expected: The person covers the 40 m in 40 s. IMO gives no tolerance.
deviations: The set walking speed is 1.2 m/s, not 1 m/s.

The person starts at a random position in the first 2 m of the corridor, and the exit is a 2 m strip at the far end (x = 38 m to 40 m) that removes the person on contact. The walked distance is therefore about 36 m to 38 m, not 40 m.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the evacuation time must lie within 20 % of 38 m / 1.2 m/s = 31.7 s, that is between 25.3 s and 38.0 s. The standard's 40 s at 1 m/s is not tested directly.
A second check requires the agent's centre to stay at least its radius, less 1 mm, inside the corridor. This check is the suite's own.
The agent uses the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m and one seed (42). The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_imo.py).

tests.title: Maintaining a set walking speed up a staircase
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 2, para. 4, p. 9
tests.definition: One person on a stair 2 m wide and 10 m long, measured along the incline, walks at a set speed of 1 m/s.
tests.expected: The person covers the 10 m in 10 s. IMO gives no tolerance. The paragraph does not say how the set speed relates to the stair speeds of Table 3.5 (Annex 3, p. 6).
deviations: The stair is a flat polygon (10.4 m by 2 m) covered by one speed-factor zone with factor 0.5. It has no incline, no steps and no direction. The test does not distinguish up from down.

The desired speed is set to 2.0 m/s, so that desired speed times zone factor equals 1 m/s on the whole polygon (decision D14). The test checks that the zone factor is applied, not that the model reproduces a stair speed from Table 3.5.
The agent starts in a 0.3 m by 0.4 m patch at the left end, and the exit is a strip 0.2 m deep and 0.4 m wide at the right end, so the walked distance is about 10 m in plan view.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the evacuation time lies between 9.5 s and 10.5 s (10 s +/- 0.5 s).
The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_imo.py); one seed (42).

tests.title: Maintaining a set walking speed down a staircase
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 3, para. 5, p. 9
tests.definition: One person on a stair 2 m wide and 10 m long, measured along the incline, walks downward at a set speed of 1 m/s. The paragraph repeats the wording of Test 2.
tests.expected: The person covers the 10 m in 10 s. IMO gives no tolerance. The paragraph does not say how the set speed relates to the stair speeds of Table 3.5 (Annex 3, p. 6).
deviations: The stair is a flat polygon (10.4 m by 2 m) covered by one speed-factor zone with factor 0.75. It has no incline, no steps and no direction. The test uses the same mechanism as Test 2 with a different constant, so it does not distinguish down from up.

The desired speed is set to 1/0.75 m/s, so that desired speed times zone factor equals 1 m/s (decision D14). The test checks that the zone factor is applied, not that the model reproduces a stair speed from Table 3.5.
The agent starts in a 0.3 m by 0.4 m patch at the left end, and the exit is a strip 0.2 m deep and 0.4 m wide at the right end, so the walked distance is about 10 m in plan view.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the evacuation time lies between 9.5 s and 10.5 s (10 s +/- 0.5 s).
The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_imo.py); one seed (42).

tests.title: Exit flow rate
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 4, para. 6, p. 9; see also Section 3.2.6, p. 6
tests.definition: 100 persons stand in a room of 8 m by 5 m. A 1 m wide exit sits at the centre of one of the 5 m walls. The flow rate measured over the whole evacuation must not exceed 1.33 p/s. Section 3.2.6 states the same limit as a specific flow of 1.33 p/m/s for any exit.
tests.expected: The flow does not exceed 1.33 p/s. The text does not define the averaging period beyond "the entire period".
deviations: The exit throughput limiter is switched on at 1.33 p/s (decision D12). The test therefore checks that the limiter holds the flow at the cap. The flow the model produces without the limiter is printed by a second test and is not asserted.
The flow is (N - 1) / (t_last - t_first) over the exit times of the 100 agents, divided by the exit width of 1 m. The standard does not name this window.
The pass rule is the suite's own: measured flow is at most 1.33 p/s plus a 1 % tolerance.
The exit is a 1 m by 1 m absorbing square inside the room, against the right-hand 5 m wall, not an opening in the wall. Agents are removed when they touch it.
The 100 agents start in the left 6 m of the room (x = 0 m to 6 m), not spread over the whole room.
Agents have a constant desired speed of 1.2 m/s and the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m; one seed (42). The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_imo.py).

tests.title: Response duration
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 5, para. 7, p. 9
tests.definition: Ten persons stand in a room of 8 m by 5 m with a 1 m exit at the centre of one 5 m wall. Their response durations are uniformly distributed between 10 s and 100 s. The test verifies that each person starts to move at the time assigned to that person.
tests.expected: Every person starts moving at the person's own assigned response duration. IMO gives no tolerance. The wording "uniformly distributed in the range" can be read as random draws from a uniform distribution or as evenly spaced values.
deviations: The response durations are random draws from a uniform distribution on 10 s to 100 s (premovement seed 12345), the first reading of the wording. Evenly spaced values are not tested.

Each agent's observed start is compared with its own assigned duration (decision D15). The scenario result does not expose the assignment, so the test assumes that agent ids ascend with spawn order and that the i-th id owns the i-th draw.

An agent starts moving at the first frame in which it is more than 0.05 m from its start position. The pass rule is the suite's own: every start lies between 9.9 s and 101 s and within 0.5 s of the assigned value.
The exit is a 1 m by 1 m absorbing square inside the room against the left 5 m wall. The agents start in a block 2 m by 3 m near the opposite wall.
Constant desired speed 1.2 m/s, default body radius 0.15 m; one seed (42). The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_imo.py).

tests.title: Rounding corners
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 6, para. 8, p. 10, Fig. 1
tests.definition: Twenty persons walk toward a left-hand corner. They start spread uniformly in a patch 4 m long and 2 m wide at the start of a corridor 2 m wide. The corridor runs 10 m, then turns left into a leg 2 m wide that continues 10 m beyond the corridor (Fig. 1, p. 10). The persons must get around the corner without penetrating the boundaries.
tests.expected: All twenty persons navigate the corner without penetrating the walls. IMO gives no numeric limit.
deviations: The leg above the corridor is 8 m long (the exit strip is at y = 8 m to 10 m), not 10 m.
The walkable polygon has a 2 m by 2 m pocket below the corridor's end that is not in Fig. 1.

The pass rule is the suite's own: all twenty agents reach the exit, and every agent's centre stays at least its radius, less 1 mm, inside the walkable polygon (decision D16). Because the polygon is not convex, the check also detects cutting across the inner corner.
Constant desired speed 1.2 m/s, default body radius 0.15 m; one seed (42). The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_imo.py).

tests.title: Assignment of population demographics
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 7, para. 9, p. 10; Table 3.4, p. 5
tests.definition: A panel of males aged 30 to 50 is taken from Table 3.4, whose walking speed on flat terrain is a uniform distribution between 0.97 m/s and 1.62 m/s. The speeds are distributed over a population of 50 persons. The test shows that the assigned speeds are consistent with the table.
tests.expected: The assigned speeds are consistent with the uniform distribution of Table 3.4 (0.97 m/s to 1.62 m/s). IMO gives no statistical test or tolerance.
deviations: No speed distribution is assigned: all 50 agents have a constant desired speed of 1.2 m/s. The test does not read or check assigned speeds against Table 3.4.
The test checks only that all 50 agents leave a 40 m by 10 m room and that the evacuation time lies between 25 s and 120 s. This window is the suite's own and is not in the standard.
Default body radius 0.15 m; one seed (42). The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_imo.py).

tests.title: Counterflow: two rooms connected by a corridor
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 8, paras. 12-14, p. 11, Fig. 2
tests.definition: Two rooms of 10 m by 10 m are joined by a corridor 10 m long and 2 m wide. The corridor starts and ends at the centre of one side of each room. The population is 100 persons with instant response and Table 3.4 speeds (males 30 to 50). Step 1: 100 persons in room 1, packed from the left wall at the highest possible density, walk to room 2. The time the last person enters room 2 is recorded. Step 2: the run is repeated with 10, 50 and 100 additional persons of the same characteristics who walk from room 2 to room 1. Both groups start together, and the time the last room-1 person enters room 2 is recorded.
tests.expected: The recorded duration increases as the number of persons in counterflow increases. IMO gives no size for the increase.
deviations: The scenario has 20 agents per room, spread over the left 8 m of room 1 (and the right 8 m of room 2), not 100 packed from the left wall.
One counterflow level (20 persons) is run against one one-way run, not the levels 10, 50 and 100. The test cannot show that the duration rises with the count.

The recorded time is the total evacuation time of the run, with exits as 2 m strips at the far walls, not the time the last room-1 person enters room 2. The counterflow run also has twice as many agents as the one-way run.
The pass rule is the suite's own: both runs complete, and the counterflow evacuation time is longer than the one-way time.

Constant desired speed 1.2 m/s instead of Table 3.4 speeds; default body radius 0.15 m; one seed (42). The room and corridor dimensions match Fig. 2. The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_imo.py).

tests.title: Exit flow: crowd dissipation from a large public room
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 9, para. 15, pp. 11-12, Fig. 3
tests.definition: A public room of 30 m by 20 m has four 1 m doors, two in each long wall at 4 m to 5 m and 25 m to 26 m from the corner (Fig. 3, p. 12). 1,000 persons with instant response and Table 3.4 speeds are distributed uniformly in the room, inset 2 m from the walls, and leave through the nearest door. Step 1: the time the last person leaves is recorded. Step 2: doors 1 and 2 are closed and step 1 is repeated.
tests.expected: Closing doors 1 and 2 roughly doubles the time to empty the room (an "approximate doubling"). IMO gives no band around two.
deviations: The population is 200 agents in the area x = 0 m to 25 m, not 1,000 agents inset 2 m on all sides.
The four exits are 1 m by 1 m absorbing squares against the right-hand 20 m wall (y = 0 m to 1 m, 5 m to 6 m, 14 m to 15 m, 19 m to 20 m), not doors in the two 30 m walls as in Fig. 3.

Agents do not choose the nearest door. Horizontal bands of the start area are assigned to one exit each through journey weights: four bands of 50 agents with four exits, two bands of 100 agents with two exits.
With two exits, the test keeps the exits at y = 0 m to 1 m and 19 m to 20 m on the same wall. In the standard the remaining doors 3 and 4 lie in one wall at 4 m to 5 m and 25 m to 26 m.
The pass rule is the suite's own: both runs complete and the two-exit time is longer than the four-exit time. The ratio to the standard's doubling is not tested.
Constant desired speed 1.2 m/s instead of Table 3.4 speeds; default body radius 0.15 m; one seed (42). The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_imo.py).

tests.title: Exit route allocation
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 10, para. 16, p. 12; Fig. 4, p. 13
tests.definition: A cabin corridor section has two rows of six cabins on either side of a corridor 0.9 m wide. The cabins are 3 m wide and 5 m deep (Fig. 4, p. 13). The population is 23 persons with instant response and Table 3.4 speeds: two persons per cabin and one person in cabin 3. A main exit, 1.2 m wide, leads out of the top row next to cabin 3. A secondary exit lies at the end of the corridor. The persons in cabins 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10 are allocated the main exit. All others are allocated the secondary exit.
tests.expected: The allocated persons move to their allocated exits. IMO gives no numeric criterion.
deviations: The scenario is loaded from the RiMEA zip standards/rimea/scenario_files/Rimea-10.zip, not from an IMO-specific file. The same zip and the same check serve RiMEA Test 10 (TestRiMEA10 in tests/vv/test_rimea.py).
The population, the cabin occupancy (2 per cabin, 1 in cabin 3) and the allocation match the standard.
The cabins are about 3.8 m deep, not 5 m, and about 2.8 m to 2.9 m wide, with cabin 3 about 1.9 m wide. The corridor is 0.9 m wide. The gap in the wall for the main exit is 1.1 m, not 1.2 m.
All 23 agents have a constant desired speed of 1.3 m/s instead of Table 3.4 speeds.

The allocation is fixed by journey weights (the standard prescribes it). An agent counts as using its allocated exit when its last recorded position is nearer to that exit than to the other one. All agents must also evacuate. Default body radius 0.15 m; one seed (42).

tests.title: Staircase
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 11, para. 17, p. 13, Fig. 5; congestion definition Sections 3.1-3.2, p. 1
tests.definition: A room of 8 m by 6 m is connected by a corridor 2 m wide and 12 m long to a stair going up (Fig. 5, p. 13). The population is 150 persons with instant response and Table 3.4 speeds, filling the room. Congestion is identified by local densities above 4 p/m2 for a significant duration (Section 3.1, p. 1), and it is significant if it lasts longer than 10 % of the total assembly time (Section 3.2).
tests.expected: Congestion forms at the exit from the room. This produces a steady flow in the corridor and congestion at the base of the stairs. IMO gives no numeric limits.
deviations: The Test 11 scenario is not implemented. There is no room, no corridor, no stair and no density or flow measurement for these locations.

The test runs the RiMEA Test 16 ring instead, with the same builder (standards/rimea/scenario_builders/rimea16_loop.py) and the same reference band file as RiMEA 16: 10 agents on a closed oval ring of 26.85 m (about 0.37 agents per metre) at desired speeds 0.9, 1.2 and 1.5 m/s.

The checks are the suite's own and come from RiMEA 16, not from IMO: every agent completes at least 3 laps; at least 75 % of the baseline (1.2 m/s) speed-density samples lie inside the RiMEA 10 %/90 % percentile band; the 0.9 m/s run is slower than the baseline; at least 75 % of the 1.5 m/s samples lie above the 90 % percentile.
The RiMEA 16 test also sweeps the agent count to high densities. This test does not.
Default body radius 0.15 m; one seed (42). The ring is built in code.

tests.title: Flow-density relation
tests.source: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1533, Annex 3, Appendix 2, Test 12, para. 18, p. 14
tests.definition: The software is tested on a corridor without obstructions. The test must demonstrate that the flow of persons in the corridor is generally smaller at very high population densities than at moderate densities.
tests.expected: Flow at very high density is smaller than flow at moderate density. IMO gives no density values and no numeric limits. The standard does not say how "very high" and "moderate" are defined.
deviations: Not implemented: the suite has no test for this row.

The ring runs of IMO 11 and RiMEA 16 measure speed against 1D density, not flow in a straight corridor. The IMO 11 run uses one agent count (about 0.37 agents per metre) and cannot show the decrease at high density. The RiMEA 16 sweep covers 1D densities of about 0.2 to 1.7 per metre and is not evaluated as flow.

tests.title: Walking speed in a corridor
tests.definition: One person walks along a corridor 2 m wide and 40 m long at a set walking speed. The test shows that the person covers the distance in the matching time. RiMEA allows for three inaccuracies: 0.4 m for body size, 1 s for premovement time and 5 % for walking speed. For a typical speed of 1.33 m/s, set between 4.5 and 5.1 km/h, this gives a travel time between 26 and 34 s.
tests.expected: The travel time at 1.33 m/s lies between 26 and 34 s. This is the only test in the guideline with a fixed window; for all other tests RiMEA states that it sets no fixed pass limits (p. 28).
deviations: The agent starts within the first 0.4 m of the corridor and is removed on entering a 0.1 m exit strip at 39.9 to 40 m, so it walks slightly less than 40 m. The window is applied to the simulated travel time without adjustment.
The suite adds a second check that RiMEA does not ask for: on every sample the agent's centre stays at least its radius, less 1 mm, inside the corridor walls (decision D16).

The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_rimea.py) with a desired speed of 1.33 m/s. The notebook loads Rimea-01-corridor.zip instead: a 60 m corridor with a 10 m run-up and a 10 m buffer, a desired speed of 1.0 m/s, and a speed measured over a 40 m segment (target 1.0 m/s, tolerance 0.05 m/s). It does not use the 26 to 34 s window.

tests.title: Walking speed up stairs
tests.source: RiMEA 4.1.1, Test 2, p. 29; stair speeds: section 3.2.2.3 and Table 3, pp. 14-15
tests.definition: One person climbs a staircase 2 m wide and 10 m long, measured along the slope, at a defined walking speed. The test shows that the person covers the distance in the corresponding time. The considerations of Test 1 apply with adjusted distance, time and speed.
tests.expected: The person covers the 10 m in the time that follows from the defined stair speed. RiMEA names no stair speed and no time window for this test; Table 3 (p. 15) gives example stair speeds after Fruin, 0.32 to 0.58 m/s upwards. RiMEA sets no fixed pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The stair is a flat corridor 2 m wide with a speed-factor zone of 0.5, not a stair object. A desired speed of 1.0 m/s then gives 0.5 m/s, inside the Fruin range for ascent. The model has no incline.
The zone covers the whole 10.4 m corridor and the agent walks about 10 m from its start to the exit strip.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the travel time lies between 19.5 and 20.5 s (10 m at 0.5 m/s is 20 s, with a tolerance of 0.5 s). RiMEA gives no window for this test.

The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_rimea.py). The notebook loads Rimea-02-upstairs.zip instead: a 30 m corridor with the speed-factor zone on 10 to 20 m only, and a speed measured over that segment (target 0.5 m/s, tolerance 0.05 m/s).

tests.title: Walking speed down stairs
tests.source: RiMEA 4.1.1, Test 3, p. 29; stair speeds: section 3.2.2.3 and Table 3, pp. 14-15
tests.definition: One person descends a staircase 2 m wide and 10 m long, measured along the slope, at a defined walking speed. The test shows that the person covers the distance in the corresponding time. The considerations of Test 1 apply with adjusted distance, time and speed.
tests.expected: The person covers the 10 m in the time that follows from the defined stair speed. RiMEA names no stair speed and no time window for this test; Table 3 (p. 15) gives example stair speeds after Fruin, 0.42 to 0.81 m/s downwards. RiMEA sets no fixed pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The stair is a flat corridor 2 m wide with a speed-factor zone of 0.75, not a stair object. A desired speed of 1.0 m/s then gives 0.75 m/s, inside the Fruin range for descent. The model has no incline.
The zone covers the whole 10.4 m corridor and the agent walks about 10 m from its start to the exit strip.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the travel time lies between 13.0 and 13.7 s (10 m at 0.75 m/s is 13.3 s). RiMEA gives no window for this test.

The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_rimea.py). The notebook loads Rimea-03-downstairs.zip instead: a 30 m corridor with a speed-factor zone of 0.65 on 10 to 20 m only, and a speed measured over that segment (target 0.65 m/s, tolerance 0.05 m/s).

tests.title: Measurement of the fundamental diagram
tests.source: RiMEA 4.1.1, Test 4, pp. 29-30, Fig. 5 (the English text calls it Figure 4)
tests.definition: A corridor 1000 m long and 10 m wide carries three measuring areas of 2 m by 2 m at about 450, 500 and 550 m. The middle area is the main one; the other two are controls. The corridor is filled with persons of nearly equal free speed (for example 1.2 to 1.4 m/s) at 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 persons per m². At each area the mean speed over 60 s is determined; the first 10 s may be dropped as a transient. The fundamental diagrams follow from the results, with flow equal to speed times density. In a second step the corridor is narrowed until persons can only walk one behind the other without overtaking, and the diagram is checked again for this line movement.
tests.expected: RiMEA names no values: the speed-density and flow-density diagrams are to be created from the measurements. It notes that empirical data exist for this test (p. 22). RiMEA sets no fixed pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The corridor is 200 m long and 10 m wide, one fifth of the specified length. The areas sit at x = 50 m (control) and x = 100 m (main, and a second control beside it), not around 450 to 550 m.
The runs use 1000, 2000, 4000 and 6000 agents, which gives about 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 persons per m². The densities 4, 5 and 6 persons per m² are not run.
The single-file line-movement case is not run.

Agents start spread over the whole corridor and walk to an exit at the downstream end. The corridor is not periodic, so the density in an area is a mean over the 10 to 60 s window and is not held fixed.

The pass rule is the suite's own: at each area the measured density rises with the agent count, and the mean speed does not rise by more than 0.05 m/s from one density level to the next. Flow is computed as speed times density and is not asserted.

tests.title: Premovement time
tests.definition: Ten persons stand in a room of 8 m by 5 m with an exit 1 m wide in the middle of a 5 m wall. Their premovement times are drawn uniformly between 10 s and 100 s. The test verifies that each person starts moving at an appropriate time.
tests.expected: Each person starts moving at a time consistent with its premovement time, which lies between 10 s and 100 s. RiMEA gives no tolerance for 'appropriate' and sets no fixed pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The pass rule is the suite's own: each agent's observed start (the first frame with a displacement above 0.05 m from its spawn point) is within 0.5 s of that agent's own sampled premovement time, and every start lies between 9.9 and 101 s.
The test pairs agents with their draws by id order, because the runner assigns ids in spawn order and the scenario result does not expose per-agent premovement times.

RiMEA does not fix where the persons start. The suite places them in a 2 m by 3 m area at the end opposite the exit, with a constant desired speed of 1.2 m/s, the default radius of 0.15 m and premovement seed 12345.

The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_rimea.py). The notebook loads Rimea-05-premovement.zip instead: a larger start area (6.6 m by 4.6 m) and a different acceptance rule, a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the start times against the uniform distribution (alpha 0.05).

tests.title: Movement around a corner
tests.source: RiMEA 4.1.1, Test 6, p. 30, Fig. 6 (p. 31; the English text calls it Figure 5)
tests.definition: Twenty persons, spread uniformly over a start area 6 m long, walk towards a corner that turns left. A corridor 10 m long and 2 m wide ends in a turn into an arm 2 m wide and 10 m long. The persons go around the corner without passing through walls.
tests.expected: All 20 persons go around the corner without passing through a wall. RiMEA states this as a yes/no outcome and sets no further pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The vertical arm runs 8 m above the corridor and 2 m below it. Fig. 6 labels a 10 m arm above the corridor and shows nothing below it.

The pass rule is the suite's own: all 20 agents evacuate, and on every sample each agent's centre stays at least its radius, less 1 mm, inside the walkable polygon, so a body overlapping the inner corner fails (decision D16).
Agents have a constant desired speed (1.2 m/s) and the default radius of 0.15 m. RiMEA's text asks for no speed.

The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_rimea.py). The notebook loads Rimea-06-corner.zip instead: a corridor 10 m long with an arm 8 m above it and no extension below, a 4 m by 2 m start area, a desired speed of 1.0 m/s, and a check of the agent centres against the polygon with a 1 mm tolerance and no radius.

tests.title: Allocation of demographic parameters
tests.source: RiMEA 4.1.1, Test 7, p. 31; Fig. 3, p. 13 (the English text of Test 7 cites Figure 2 and a table, the German text cites Abb. 3)
tests.definition: A group of adults is chosen from Fig. 3, which gives mean walking speed on level ground as a function of age after Weidmann, with a band of one standard deviation. Walking speeds are distributed over a population of 50 persons. The test shows that the distribution of simulated walking speeds is consistent with the distribution in the figure.
tests.expected: The simulated speed distribution is consistent with Fig. 3. RiMEA gives no measure of agreement and sets no fixed pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The population has 50 adults at the ages 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70 years (10, 10, 10, 10, 5 and 5 persons); the age mix is the suite's own choice. Each age gets speeds inside a band 0.04 m/s wide around the mean curve of Fig. 3 (single values of 1.27 and 1.07 m/s at ages 60 and 70). The spread of about 0.3 m/s near age 20 shown in Fig. 3 is not reproduced.

The pass rule is the suite's own: assigned speeds lie in the age band, the median observed speed of each agent lies in the band within 0.03 m/s, and the mean observed speed does not rise with age. The observed speeds come from free walking in a room of 70 m by 20 m, so the test shows that agents reach their assigned speed.

tests.title: Parameter study on a three-storey plan
tests.definition: On the three-storey floor plan of Fig. 7, with four persons in each room, the total evacuation time is determined while one person parameter at a time is varied and the others stay at fixed standard values. Each parameter is varied twice: once equal for all persons (for example speed 0.5, 0.75 or 1.0 m/s) and once spread uniformly around a fixed mean (for example 0.5 to 1.0 m/s around 0.75 m/s). The results are recorded in graphs.
tests.expected: RiMEA gives no expected values: it asks for graphs of the total evacuation time against each parameter, to be published on the RiMEA homepage. RiMEA sets no fixed pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The building has 3 floors with 10 rooms of 3 m by 3 m each (two rows of five along a corridor 2 m wide) and four persons per room, 120 agents in total. Fig. 7 has four rows of rooms per floor and more than 100 persons per floor.
The stairs are flat boxes of 2 m by 3 m that join the floors, with no speed reduction. There is one exit at the end of the ground-floor corridor.

Only the desired speed is varied. The constant values are 1.0, 1.25, 1.5 and 2.0 m/s, and the spread cases are uniform around 1.25 m/s with half-ranges of 0.25 and 0.5 m/s. RiMEA's examples start at 0.5 m/s. Other parameters are not varied.

The pass rule is the suite's own: the evacuation time falls strictly as the constant speed rises, and each spread case is within 30 % of the constant 1.25 m/s run. The test writes no graphs. All runs use seed 42.

tests.title: Crowd leaving a large public space
tests.source: RiMEA 4.1.1, Test 9, p. 34, Fig. 8, footnotes 7 and 8
tests.definition: A public space of 30 m by 20 m has four doors, each 1 m wide: two in the top wall and two in the bottom wall, 4 m from the side walls. A population of 1000 adults from Fig. 3, with immediate reaction, is spread evenly over the room and its speeds are distributed over the 1000 persons. Step 1 records the time at which the last person leaves. In step 2 doors 1 and 2 (the top doors) are locked and step 1 is repeated.
tests.expected: RiMEA expects the time to leave the room to roughly double with two doors locked. Footnote 7 (p. 34) says denser queues in front of the doors may raise the flow, so the test is not to be used as an exclusion criterion and only documents model behaviour. RiMEA sets no pass limit.
deviations: The pass rule is the suite's own (decision D22): all agents evacuate in both runs and the evacuation with two exits takes longer than with four. The ratio of the two times is reported and is not asserted.

The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_rimea.py) as a room of 20 m by 20 m with four exits 2 m wide at the centre of each wall, and 200 agents with a constant desired speed of 1.2 m/s. The two-exit case keeps the bottom and top exits. The notebook loads Rimea-09-large-public.zip and Rimea-09-large-public-locked.zip instead: 30 m by 20 m, doors 1 m wide as in Fig. 8, 1000 agents with Gaussian speeds (mean 1.6 m/s, standard deviation 0.2 m/s), and the top doors removed in the second run.

Agents do not choose a door. Journey weights fix the exit of each group: in the test every spawn quadrant has one exit, so some groups cross the room; in the scenario files the weights split the agents evenly over the open doors.
Agents have no premovement time, the default radius of 0.15 m and one seed (42). The speeds are not drawn from the RiMEA population of Fig. 3.

tests.title: Allocation of escape routes
tests.definition: A corridor section with 12 adjacent rooms (Fig. 9) holds 23 adults from Fig. 3 with immediate reaction: two persons in each room and one in room 3. The persons in rooms 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10 are assigned to the main exit and all others to the secondary exit. Walking speeds are distributed over the 23 persons.
tests.expected: All persons go to the exit they are assigned to. This is a yes/no outcome; RiMEA gives no numeric limits (p. 28).
deviations: Walking speeds are constant (1.3 m/s) and not drawn from the population of Fig. 3. Agents use the default radius of 0.15 m and one seed (42).

The pass rule is the suite's own: all agents evacuate, and each agent's last recorded position is nearest to the exit it was assigned to. Each room has its own journey fixed to its exit, so the test shows that assigned routes are followed.

tests.title: Choice of escape route
tests.definition: A public space of 30 m by 20 m has two exits, each 1 m wide, in the top wall: exit 1 at 21 m from the left wall and exit 2 5 m to its right. A population of 1000 adults from Fig. 3 with immediate reaction occupies the space from the left side at the maximum possible density, with a 2 m margin to the left and bottom walls. Walking speeds are distributed over the 1000 persons.
tests.expected: Most persons prefer the closer exit 1 and congestion forms in front of it, but some persons also use exit 2. RiMEA sets no numeric limit for 'most' or 'some' (p. 28).
deviations: The test, not the simulator, chooses the exit. Before the run each agent draws its exit from a logistic function of the distance difference to the two exit centres (scale 3 m) with a seeded random generator, and is then routed to that exit. The assertions (more agents at exit 1 than at exit 2, and at least one at exit 2) count these draws. The simulation checks only that all agents evacuate. Congestion at exit 1 is not checked.
The notebook uses the same scenario file and the same choice model. It counts exit use from the last recorded positions and requires at least 55 % of the agents at exit 1.

The 1000 agents have a constant desired speed (1.2 m/s) and the default radius of 0.15 m. They start in an area of 16 m by 16 m at 2 to 18 m from the left and bottom walls, a density of about 3.9 persons per m². RiMEA asks for the maximum possible density and Fig. 10 dimensions only the 2 m margins. The exits are 1.1 m wide.

tests.title: Position of the goal behind a bottleneck
tests.definition: Two rooms are joined by a single bottleneck. 150 agents of the RiMEA standard population, with no response time, start in room 1. Their goal lies in room 2 at a distance a behind the bottleneck. Several runs vary a from 0 to 10 m, and the time needed to clear room 1 is determined as a function of a. The background: when agents are removed on reaching their goal, the goal's distance to the last bottleneck can change the evacuation time.
tests.expected: RiMEA describes the usual behaviour: the evacuation time is shortest when the goal sits directly behind the last bottleneck, and it grows with a until it reaches a constant value. RiMEA sets no pass limit.
deviations: The pass rule is the suite's own (decision D21): every a of 1 m or more clears room 1 later than a = 0.2 m, and the mean over a of 4 m or more is not below the value at a = 1 m.
The smallest goal distance is 0.2 m, because the goal is a 0.2 m wide strip.
All agents walk at one constant desired speed of 1.2 m/s; RiMEA's standard population derives speeds from age.
Agents use the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m and one seed (42). RiMEA's standard population defines sex and age only, not body size.

tests.title: Length of a bottleneck
tests.definition: Two geometries each consist of two rooms of 10 m by 10 m joined by a bottleneck 1 m wide: a door in a wall 0.2 m thick, and a bottleneck 5 m long. 150 agents of the RiMEA standard population, with no response time, start in the left 5 m of room 1. Their goal lies at the right edge of room 2. The background: lab data (Fig. 12) show that the length of a bottleneck affects the flow, because slower persons hold up faster ones. The test shows that the time to clear room 1 is larger for the long bottleneck.
tests.expected: The room-1 clearance time is larger for the long bottleneck than for the short one. RiMEA states the direction only and sets no pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The room-1 clearance time is the time the last agent crosses the line at x = 10 m, the entrance of the bottleneck (decision D9), not the total evacuation time. The pass rule is the suite's own: the long bottleneck takes longer, with one run per geometry and no margin.

Agents have one desired speed (1.2 m/s), the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m and one seed (42). RiMEA's standard population (section 3.2.4, p. 16) defines sex and age; speeds follow from age (Fig. 3, p. 13) and body size is not defined.

tests.title: Influence of congestion
tests.definition: Three rooms in a row, 10 m, 10 m and 5 m long and 10 m wide, are joined by two identical bottlenecks, each 1 m wide and 0.2 m long. 150 agents of the RiMEA standard population, with no response time, start in the left 5 m of room 1. Their goal lies at the right edge of room 3. The background: hand calculations treat the flow as a function of bottleneck width, while a microscopic simulation also captures interactions in the queue in front of a bottleneck. The test determines the number of agents in rooms 1 and 2 over time and the flows through bottlenecks 1 and 2.
tests.expected: RiMEA names no values and no pass limit. It asks for the time course of the agent numbers in rooms 1 and 2 and for the flows in bottlenecks 1 and 2 to be determined and documented.
deviations: The pass rule is the suite's own (decision D17): only conservation is asserted. At every sampled frame the agents in rooms 1 to 3 and in the two bottlenecks, plus the agents already evacuated, add up to 150. The flow through each bottleneck and the peak number of agents in room 2 are reported and are not asserted. The notebook plots the agent count per room over time and the cumulative crossings at each bottleneck.
The flow is the number of agents minus one, divided by the time between the first and the last first-crossing of the bottleneck's measurement line. RiMEA does not define a flow measure.

The scenario file deviates slightly from Fig. 14: room 2 is about 9.8 m and room 3 about 4.8 m long, the bottlenecks are about 1.0 m wide, and the goal is a strip at 24.1 to 24.8 m rather than at the right edge.

Agents have one desired speed (1.2 m/s), the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m and one seed (42). RiMEA's standard population (section 3.2.4, p. 16) defines sex and age; speeds follow from age (Fig. 3, p. 13) and body size is not defined.

tests.title: Bottleneck width and flow
tests.source: RiMEA 4.1.1, Test 12d, p. 41, Figs. 13 (lower geometry) and 15
tests.definition: The lower geometry of Fig. 13 has two rooms of 10 m by 10 m joined by a bottleneck 5 m long. The bottleneck width w is varied over 0.8, 1.0 and 1.2 m. 150 agents of the RiMEA standard population, with no response time, start in room 1 and the goal lies at the right edge of room 2. Real-life tests (Fig. 15) show the flow rising with the width. The test shows that the simulated flow rises with w.
tests.expected: The flow increases with the bottleneck width. RiMEA names no flow values and sets no pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The test uses 50 agents, not 150.

The test takes the flow as the number of agents divided by the total evacuation time of the run, which includes the walk to the bottleneck and on to the goal, so it is not a flow measured at the bottleneck. The notebook measures the mean flow at the bottleneck line x = 10 m with PedPy and compares it with the line J = 1.9 w.
The pass rule is the suite's own: flow(0.8 m) < flow(1.0 m) < flow(1.2 m), with one run per width.

The goal is a strip 2 m deep at 23 to 25 m rather than a line at the right edge. Agents have one desired speed (1.2 m/s), the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m and one seed (42). RiMEA's standard population (section 3.2.4, p. 16) defines sex and age; speeds follow from age (Fig. 3, p. 13) and body size is not defined.
The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_rimea.py). The notebook loads Rimea-12d-bottleneck.zip, the 1.0 m case, and changes the width in memory for the other cases.

tests.title: Fundamental diagram on stairs
tests.source: RiMEA 4.1.1, Test 13, pp. 42-43, Figs. 16 and 17; stair speeds: Table 3, p. 15
tests.definition: Two geometries differ only in the direction of the stair (Fig. 17): a room of 10 m by 10 m opens into a corridor 2 m wide that holds a stair 5 m long between a 2 m approach and a 2 m exit leg. The captions of Fig. 17 disagree (German: downwards, English: upwards); the sketch serves both directions. 100 agents of the RiMEA standard population, with no response time, start in the room and walk to the goal. Speed and density refer to the horizontally projected stair area. Field data (Fig. 16) show lower speeds upwards than downwards. The test shows that the walking speeds lie within the spread of Fig. 16 and that they are higher downwards than upwards.
tests.expected: The speeds lie within the spread of the field data in Fig. 16 and are higher on the way down than on the way up. RiMEA sets no further pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The stair is a flat zone of 5 m by 2 m in the corridor with speed factors of 0.5 (up) and 0.7 (down), not a stair object. That the downward speed exceeds the upward speed is largely set by these input factors.

The 100 agents form seven groups with desired speeds from 0.96 to 1.34 m/s, labelled after the groups of Table 3. This is not the RiMEA standard population (section 3.2.4, p. 16: 50 % men and 50 % women, age normally distributed with mean 50 and standard deviation 20 years, 10 to 85 years). Agents have the default radius of 0.15 m.

The spread of Fig. 16 is replaced by a coded envelope (mean plus or minus one standard deviation of a fast and a slow sub-population, function corbetta_envelope_bounds in standards/rimea/scenario_builders/rimea13_stairs.py). Its coefficients are not yet checked against Fig. 16.

The pass rule is the suite's own (decision D13): at least 25 % of the speed samples of each direction lie inside the coded envelope, at least 70 % of the shared density bins (0.6 to 1.5 persons per m²) show a higher speed downwards, and the mean over those bins is higher downwards. The test publishes the fraction inside the envelope for each direction. RiMEA asks for all speeds to lie within the spread.

tests.title: Choice of route
tests.definition: A start area and a target area are joined by two flights of stairs and a corridor on the ground floor, which is the shorter route, and by a longer corridor on the upper floor. The test documents whether the pedestrians take the shorter route via another storey or stay on the longer route on one storey. The answer is one of 'short', 'long', 'mixed' or 'configurable'.
tests.expected: RiMEA names no expected route: it asks for one of the four answers to be documented. It sets no pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The scenario is a single-level 2D hall with a start area and a target area and no stairs or storeys, so there is no stair-speed trade-off between the routes.

Agents do not choose between routes. The long route is set by a chain of five checkpoints that the agents visit before the exit, and the direct route has only the exit. The result supports the answer 'configurable'.

The test replaces the scenario's flow spawning (100 agents) with a batch of 30 agents and counts an agent on the long route when its largest y exceeds 12 m. The pass rule is the suite's own: with the direct journey all 30 agents take the short route, and with the checkpoint journey more agents take the long route than the short one.

tests.title: Large crowd around a corner
tests.definition: Three geometries, each 20 m wide with a start area of 20 m by 6 m, hold 500 persons; the same group of persons is used in each. The geometries are a straight route of 75.4 m (the longest), a straight route of 44 m (the shortest) and a route with a corner whose dimensions Fig. 19 gives (34 m leg, then a turning area 30 m wide). The time until all persons reach the target is compared, to show how much a corner changes the evacuation time.
tests.expected: Ideally the time for the corner geometry lies between the times for the 44 m and the 75.4 m straight routes. RiMEA sets no fixed pass limit (p. 28).
deviations: The test builds two geometries, not three: a straight corridor 55 m long and an L-shaped corridor of about the same path length, both 6 m wide. It has 100 agents with a constant desired speed (1.2 m/s) and the default radius of 0.15 m. The start areas differ (6 m by 6 m and 5 m by 4 m), so the initial conditions are not identical. One seed (42).

The pass rule is the suite's own: all agents evacuate and the corner geometry takes longer than the straight one. This is a different claim from RiMEA's bracket between the shortest and the longest route.

The notebook loads three scenario files (Rimea-15-large-crowd-corner-1.zip to -3.zip): 20 m wide geometries of 81.4 m and 50 m straight length and a curved corner geometry, with 500 agents, and checks the bracket. The test does not use them.

tests.title: 1D fundamental diagram
tests.definition: The mean walking speed of all agents in a measuring range is determined for varying densities, with the density given in persons per metre. The geometry is a ring (Fig. 21: two straights of 4 m and two half circles of radius 3 m) or a corridor of about 200 m (Fig. 22), narrow enough that agents move freely but cannot overtake. On the ring the agents walk several laps and there is no exit. Two or three agent profiles with constant speeds are defined (for example 1 m/s) to show how the model parameters change the curve. The reference is the 10 % and 90 % percentile band of real-life data (Fig. 20).
tests.expected: The curves for the different profiles show the influence of the parameters, with the real-life 10 % and 90 % percentiles as the reference. RiMEA sets no pass limit (p. 28). The raw data are at doi 10.5281/zenodo.8378592 and the percentile table is on rimea.de (p. 49).
deviations: Only the ring is used. The lane is 0.8 m wide, which fits two agents of 0.3 m diameter side by side, so the geometry does not prevent overtaking. The test counts frames in which the cyclic order of the agents changes.

The density sweep puts 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 45 agents on the ring (a track of about 26.85 m, so about 0.2 to 1.7 persons per metre) at a desired speed of 1.2 m/s, for 180 s per run with the first lap discarded. Separate runs with 10 agents at 0.9, 1.2 and 1.5 m/s walk at least three laps. Density per agent is taken from the gaps to its two neighbours along the ring. Agents have the default radius of 0.15 m and one seed (42).

The pass rule is the suite's own (decision D11): no change of order at any level, mean speed not rising with the agent count (tolerance 0.02 m/s per step) and falling by at least 0.5 m/s from the lowest to the highest count, at least 75 % of the density-binned speeds inside the 10 to 90 % band, the 0.9 m/s run slower than the 1.2 m/s run, and at least 75 % of the 1.5 m/s bins above the 90 % percentile.
The reference band is read from a CSV copy of RiMEA's percentile table (standards/rimea/scenario_files/rimea16_percentile_reference.csv).

tests.title: Pre-evacuation time distributions
tests.definition: A room of 8 m by 5 m has a 1 m exit. Ten occupants are placed at random positions in it. Each pre-evacuation time distribution that the model offers (for example uniform, normal or log-normal) is assigned to the occupants in turn, and the test is repeated for every such distribution. It is a modified version of IMO Test 5. The test checks that the model assigns the pre-evacuation times as specified.
tests.expected: Each occupant starts moving at its assigned time, and the responses of the population fall within the specified range. The tester chooses a quantitative method to compare the simulated and the assigned distributions. TN 1822 asks for several runs of the same scenario, because the required number of runs depends on the distribution.
deviations: The suite tests four distributions: uniform U(10, 100) s, gamma, log-normal and Weibull. TN 1822 names only the types, so the parameters (gamma shape 1.291 and scale 103.901, log-normal 4.586 and 0.967, Weibull scale 139.285 and shape 1.195) are the suite's choice. A normal distribution, which the standard names as an example, is not run.
The pass rule is the suite's own: a one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the observed start times against the assigned distribution must give p > 0.05.
Each case is one run with 10 occupants (seed 42). TN 1822 asks for repeated runs, and a sample of 10 gives the test little power to separate distributions.
The start time of an occupant is the first frame in which it has moved more than 0.05 m from its spawn point, so it is measured from the trajectory and not read from the model input.
Occupants are placed in a 6.6 m by 4.6 m area inside the room, use the constant desired speed 1.2 m/s and the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m.

tests.title: Speed in a corridor
tests.definition: One occupant with an assigned walking speed of 1 m/s walks along a corridor of 2 m by 40 m. The test checks that the model keeps an assigned walking speed over time. It is based on IMO Test 1.
tests.expected: The occupant covers the corridor in 40 s. The result is a quantitative comparison of the simulated and the expected time. For grid-based models TN 1822 asks for at least two orientations of the geometry (for example 0 and 45 degrees), and for a check of the sensitivity to cell size.
deviations: The corridor is 60 m long: a 10 m buffer at each end surrounds the 40 m measurement segment, so the occupant has reached its desired speed when timing starts. The speed is taken from the time between x = 10 m and x = 50 m.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the measured speed must be within 0.05 m/s of 1.0 m/s, which equals a time of 38.1 s to 42.1 s over 40 m. TN 1822 sets no tolerance.
The test runs one orientation and one seed (42). The orientation and cell-size checks are written for grid-based models and do not apply to the continuous-space model.
The occupant has the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m and starts in a 1 m by 0.5 m box at the corridor entrance.

tests.title: Speed on stairs, downward
tests.definition: One occupant with a walking speed of 1 m/s walks downward along a stair that is 2 m wide and 100 m long, measured along the incline. The test checks that the model keeps an assigned speed on stairs. It is based on IMO Test 3 (downward); IMO Test 2 is the upward case.
tests.expected: The occupant covers the 100 m in 100 s. The result is a quantitative comparison of the simulated and the expected time. TN 1822 allows a model to run only one of the upward and downward tests when it uses the same input for both directions, and asks network models to show the sensitivity to the network and to the rotation of the geometry.
deviations: Stairs are not modelled. The scenario is a flat corridor of 120 m by 2 m with no stair element, speed zone or speed factor, so the test repeats Verif.2.1 over a 100 m segment and exercises no stair behaviour.
The corridor is 120 m long: a 10 m buffer at each end surrounds the 100 m measurement segment.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the measured speed must be within 0.05 m/s of 1.0 m/s, which equals a time of 95.2 s to 105.3 s over 100 m. TN 1822 sets no tolerance.
The test runs one seed (42) with the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m.
The occupant walks in the -x direction, from about x = 119 m to the exit at x = 0 m, through the same flat corridor shape as the upward case.

tests.title: Speed on stairs, upward
tests.definition: One occupant with a walking speed of 1 m/s walks upward along a stair that is 2 m wide and 100 m long, measured along the incline. The test checks that the model keeps an assigned speed on stairs. It is based on IMO Test 2 (upward); IMO Test 3 is the downward case.
tests.expected: The occupant covers the 100 m in 100 s. The result is a quantitative comparison of the simulated and the expected time. TN 1822 allows a model to run only one of the upward and downward tests when it uses the same input for both directions, and asks network models to show the sensitivity to the network and to the rotation of the geometry.
deviations: Stairs are not modelled. The scenario is a flat corridor of 120 m by 2 m with no stair element, speed zone or speed factor, so the test repeats Verif.2.1 over a 100 m segment and exercises no stair behaviour.
The corridor is 120 m long: a 10 m buffer at each end surrounds the 100 m measurement segment.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the measured speed must be within 0.05 m/s of 1.0 m/s, which equals a time of 95.2 s to 105.3 s over 100 m. TN 1822 sets no tolerance.
The test runs one seed (42) with the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m.
The occupant walks in the +x direction from about x = 1 m to the exit at x = 120 m.

tests.title: Movement around a corner
tests.definition: Twenty occupants are spread evenly over a 4 m by 2 m area at one end of an L-shaped hallway that is 2 m wide. The horizontal leg is 10 m long and the vertical leg is 10 m long, measured as in Fig. 1. Occupants have no pre-evacuation time and walk at 1 m/s. It is the layout of IMO Test 6. The test checks that the model keeps occupants inside the boundaries of the geometry.
tests.expected: The occupants navigate the corner without penetrating the boundaries. The evaluation is qualitative: the tester inspects the paths of the occupants, with the model's visualisation or the recorded coordinates. TN 1822 states that the test checks the boundaries only and does not check the movement pattern in the corner.
deviations: The legs are 2 m shorter than in Fig. 1: the geometry is 10 m by 10 m overall, so the horizontal leg is 8 m plus the 2 m width of the vertical leg, and the vertical leg rises 8 m above the horizontal one. The population area (4 m by 2 m), the hallway width and the exit at the top of the vertical leg follow the figure.

The pass rule is the suite's own: all 20 occupants evacuate, the evacuation time is below 60 s, and the centre of every occupant stays at least its radius (0.15 m) minus 1 mm inside the walkable area, so a body does not overlap a wall. TN 1822 asks for a visual check and names no limit.
The test runs one seed (42).

tests.title: Assigned occupant demographics
tests.definition: A square room of 100 m by 100 m holds 100 occupants spread evenly. Their walking speeds are assigned from a population chosen to match the building's expected occupants. The test checks that the model assigns these demographic parameters correctly; it is a modified version of IMO Test 7.
tests.expected: The walking speeds used in the simulation are consistent with the distribution specified in the scenario. The tester chooses a suitable quantitative method to compare the simulated and assigned distributions.
deviations: The test reads the scenario file and checks the configured Gaussian(1.2, 0.2) m/s desired-speed distribution. It runs no simulation and samples no agent, so it verifies the input, not the model's assignment.

tests.title: Reduced visibility vs walking speed
tests.definition: A corridor of 2 m by 100 m has a 1 m wide exit at the end. One occupant has an unimpeded speed of 1.25 m/s in clear air. A constant extinction coefficient K_s of 1.0 /m is applied in the whole corridor before the run, with no light sources. The occupant walks to the exit. Models describe the effect of smoke on speed with one of five correlations (Eqs. 1-5 of TN 1822, from Ronchi et al. 2013a), which are fractional or absolute speed reductions, with or without a minimum speed in dense smoke (about 0.3 to 0.4 m/s). Only the effect of reduced visibility on walking speed is tested, not irritant or toxic effects.
tests.expected: The travel time equals the time that the tester calculates by hand with the correlation of the model, that is, with the model's own speed reduction factor. The result is a quantitative comparison of times. TN 1822 asks to repeat the test for other combinations of clear-air speed (1.0, 0.75, 0.5 and 0.25 m/s) and extinction coefficient (10, 7.5, 3.0 and 0.5 /m). A model without a smoke-speed sub-model should describe that limitation, including that it cannot follow visibility changing over time.
deviations: JuPedSim has no smoke or visibility model. A test-side adapter turns K_s into a speed factor before the run and writes it as the factor of a zone that covers the corridor. The adapter uses the form of Eq. 2, v = max(v_min, v0 c(K_s)), with c(K_s) = 1 - 0.5 K_s and v_min = 0.3 m/s. At K_s = 1 /m, c = 0.5, the speed is 0.625 m/s and the expected time over 100 m is 160 s.

What is verified: the simulated occupant crosses a speed-factor zone at the factor's speed. What is not verified: a smoke model, the correlation itself (c(K_s) = 1 - 0.5 K_s is the suite's choice, not a published correlation), the dependence on K_s, or smoke that varies in space or time. At K_s = 1 /m the minimum speed does not apply, so that branch of Eq. 2 is not exercised.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the time over the 100 m segment must be within 0.5 s of the hand calculation. TN 1822 sets no tolerance.
Only one of the 16 suggested combinations of clear-air speed and extinction coefficient is run, with one seed (42).

The corridor is 120 m long, with a 10 m buffer at each end of the 100 m measurement segment. The 1 m exit is the capture area at the corridor end. The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_nist.py) rather than loaded from a scenario file.

tests.title: Occupant incapacitation
tests.definition: One occupant stands in the centre of a room of 10 m by 10 m by 3 m with no fire. A pre-evacuation time above 10,000,000 s keeps the occupant in place. Hazardous conditions, such as CO, HCN, CO2, irritants, heat or radiation, are applied according to the incapacitation sub-model of the evacuation model. The time at which the model's Fractional Effective Dose (FED) reaches 1 is compared with the same time from a hand calculation or an independent fire model that uses the same FED equations at the occupant's position. The test is a modified version of a test of Korhonen and Hostikka (2009).
tests.expected: The time to FED = 1 in the evacuation model equals the time in the hand calculation or fire model. The result is a quantitative comparison of the two times. TN 1822 asks to repeat the test for each hazardous condition of the sub-model, and states that a model without a toxicity or hazard sub-model should describe that limitation. The test is static, and testers may extend it to a moving occupant.
deviations: JuPedSim has no hazard, FED or incapacitation model. A test-side adapter integrates the FDS+Evac FED (Korhonen and Hostikka 2009) on every time step (dt = 0.05 s) for constant CO = 5000 ppm, CO2 = 2 % and O2 = 18 %: the CO dose rate 4.607e-7 C^1.036 per second (C in ppm), multiplied by the CO2 factor exp(0.1930 c + 2.0004) / 7.1 (c in %), plus the low-O2 rate 1 / (60 exp(8.13 - 0.54 (20.9 - O2))) per second. When FED reaches 1 the adapter sets the desired speed to zero. This gives FED = 1 after about 208 s.

What is verified: the time integration of the adapter, that is, the step on which the sum crosses 1 is the first step at or after the closed-form time 1 / (total rate) and at most one time step later, and the occupant stays at its position. What is not verified: the FED model against an independent source (the reference uses the same equations), JuPedSim itself, or any hazard in a spatially or temporally varying field.
Only the combined CO, CO2 and O2 condition is run. TN 1822 asks for each hazardous condition separately, and other hazards (HCN, heat, irritants) are not implemented.

The occupant is held at (5, 5) m by a waiting stage that never ends. This is the same as a pre-evacuation time above 10,000,000 s without running that long. The room is two-dimensional, so its 3 m height is not represented.
The scenario is built in code (tests/vv/test_nist.py) rather than loaded from a scenario file.

tests.title: Elevator usage
tests.definition: Two rooms lie on different floors, 3.5 m apart, and are joined only by an elevator. One occupant with an unimpeded walking speed of 1 m/s and no response time starts in room 2. The elevator starts at room 1, travels to room 2, picks up the occupant and returns to room 1, where the occupant leaves through a 1 m exit. The tester defines the elevator's kinematics.
tests.expected: The occupant first enters the elevator in room 2, is then discharged in room 1, and reaches the exit of room 1. A model without an elevator sub-model should document this limitation.
deviations: Not implemented: JuPedSim has no elevator component.

tests.title: Horizontal counter-flows in rooms
tests.definition: Two 10 m by 10 m rooms are joined by a 10 m long, 2 m wide corridor. 100 occupants with no response time fill room 1 from the left at the highest possible density and move to room 2; the time the last of them enters room 2 is recorded. The run is repeated with 10, 50 and 100 additional occupants in room 2 who move to room 1 at the same time and have the same characteristics.
tests.expected: The recorded time increases with the number of people in counter-flow. The tester discusses qualitatively how large the increase is.
deviations: Decision D10: a level at which room-1 occupants block and do not all reach room 2 within the time budget is reported as 'blocking documented', as ISO 20414 asks for the same scenario, and counts as later than any level that completes.
Desired speed is a constant 1.2 m/s instead of a building-population distribution.

tests.title: Group behaviours
tests.definition: A 15 m by 20 m room has a 1 m exit. Group 1 is five able-bodied adults at the top of the room with no response time: four walk at 1.25 m/s and one at 0.5 m/s. Ten slower adults (Group 2, 0.2 m/s) stand spread over the centre of the room. The occupants of Group 1 must reach the exit. The test asks whether the model can keep a group together even when its members have different walking speeds.
tests.expected: The members of Group 1 reach the exit together: their arrival times differ by no more than 10 s. TN 1822 states that the 10 s value is a chosen number to allow a quantitative comparison. A model without a group sub-model should document this limitation.
deviations: Zone 1 lies against the right-hand wall rather than at the top centre of the room as in Fig. 6.

tests.title: People with movement disabilities
tests.definition: Room 1 (5 m by 4 m, 1 m above ground) and room 2 (5 m long, at ground level) are joined by a ramp 2 m long and 1.5 m wide. A 1 m wide exit is at the end of room 2. Scenario 1: 24 occupants in zone 1 of room 1 have an unimpeded speed of 1.25 m/s and the default body size of the model. One disabled occupant in zone 2 (a 1 m strip of room 1 at the ramp) walks at 0.8 m/s on horizontal surfaces and 0.4 m/s on the ramp, and occupies more than half the ramp width (above 0.75 m), for example a wheelchair user. Scenario 2: zone 2 holds an occupant like the 24 others. All occupants must reach the exit. The test needs a model that gives agents different sizes.
tests.expected: Occupants of zone 1 reach the exit later in Scenario 1 than in Scenario 2. The evaluation is qualitative: the tester judges whether the model can simulate disabled occupants and their effect on evacuation times. A model without this feature should describe that limitation.
deviations: The pass rule is the suite's own (decision D8): all 25 occupants evacuate in both scenarios, and both the last and the mean exit time of the 24 zone-1 occupants are strictly later in Scenario 1. TN 1822 does not say which statistic of the zone-1 times to compare. The evacuation time of the disabled occupant itself is not used.
The 1 m level difference is not modelled: the rooms and the ramp are flat. The ramp is a 2 m by 1.5 m region of the floor plan.

The disabled occupant has a body radius of 0.4 m (0.8 m wide) and desired speeds of 0.8 m/s outside the ramp and 0.4 m/s on it. The suite's builder (standards/utils/movement_disability.py) sets this desired speed on every step from the occupant's position, because jupedsim-scenarios 0.7.3 applies a speed zone to every agent. The 24 zone-1 occupants keep 1.25 m/s everywhere and the default radius of 0.15 m.
The test runs one seed (42) with CollisionFreeSpeedModel set to neighbour repulsion strength 2.6 and range 0.1. The scenario is built in code rather than loaded from a scenario file.

tests.title: Exit route allocation
tests.definition: Twelve rooms of 3.0 m by 5.0 m lie on both sides of a 1.0 m wide corridor, with 0.9 m wide doors, as in Fig. 8. The rooms hold 23 occupants: two in each room except room 3, which holds one. They have no pre-evacuation time and speeds that follow the expected demographics of the building. Occupants of rooms 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 10 are allocated to the main exit and those of rooms 5, 6, 11 and 12 to the secondary exit. The test is based on IMO Test 10 and verifies the assignment of exits.
tests.expected: Every occupant moves to its allocated exit. The evaluation is qualitative, by visual inspection if possible. The tester states whether the exit choice of the model is deterministic or predictive.
deviations: The geometry is the layout of the RiMEA Test 10 scenario. Read from geometry.wkt, the rooms are about 3 m wide and 3.9 m deep (Fig. 8: 5.0 m) and the corridor is about 0.9 m wide (Fig. 8: 1.0 m). The main exit lies above room 3 and the secondary exit at the end of the corridor, as in the figure.
The allocation is an input. Each room has its own journey that ends at its exit, so the test verifies that occupants follow their assigned journey and not that the model chooses an exit.
The pass rule is the suite's own: all 23 occupants evacuate, and each one leaves through the exit that its journey assigns (100 % match). TN 1822 asks for a visual check.
All occupants have the constant desired speed 1.3 m/s and the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m. TN 1822 asks for speeds from a population distribution.
The test runs one seed (42).

tests.title: Social influence
tests.definition: A room of 10 m by 15 m has two 1 m wide exits on the 15 m walls, with their centres 12 m from the bottom 10 m wall. Scenario 1: one occupant (occupant 1) without pre-evacuation time, walking at 1 m/s, stands 1 m from the bottom wall at the same position in every run, equidistant from both exits and with no preferred exit. Scenario 2: a second occupant stands 2 m from the bottom wall and is assigned to Exit 2. Each scenario is repeated until the exit usage changes by no more than 1 % with one more run. The test needs an exit-choice model that includes social interaction.
tests.expected: The usage of Exit 2 by occupant 1 is higher in Scenario 2 than in Scenario 1. The result is a quantitative comparison of exit usage. A model whose exit choice is a user input or the shortest distance should document that limitation, because it then always chooses the closest exit.
deviations: The criterion is not met by this model. CollisionFreeSpeedModel has no social-influence mechanism, so the two free occupants draw their exit from fixed 50/50 journey weights, independent of other occupants, and the Exit 2 usage in Scenario 2 is not raised.

Scenario 1 has two free occupants instead of one. They start at random positions in a 1.3 m by 1.0 m area around x = 5 m, 0.5 m to 1.5 m from the bottom wall, instead of one fixed position. Scenario 2 adds one occupant, assigned to Exit 2, at about 2 m from the bottom wall.

The pass rule is the suite's own: over 40 seeds (1 to 40), the Exit 2 fraction of the two free occupants in Scenario 2 must be larger than in Scenario 1. TN 1822 asks to repeat until the usage changes by no more than 1 %, and the suite uses a fixed number of seeds.
Occupants use the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m.

tests.title: Affiliation
tests.definition: The room of Verif.3.2 is used: 10 m by 15 m, with two 1 m wide exits on the 15 m walls, equidistant from the bottom wall. Scenario 1: one occupant without pre-evacuation time, walking at 1 m/s, is unfamiliar with both exits and stands at the same position in every run, equidistant from the exits. Scenario 2: one occupant at the start of the corridor area is affiliated with Exit 2, which it prefers when everything else is equal for both exits. Each scenario is repeated until the exit usage changes by no more than 1 % with one more run. The test needs an exit-choice model with a variable for affiliation (familiarity) with exits.
tests.expected: The usage of Exit 2 in Scenario 2 is higher than in Scenario 1. The result is a quantitative comparison of exit usage. When exit choice is deterministic (distance only or user input), TN 1822 treats the test as an analytical verification of model assignment and not as emergent behaviour. The tester documents whether the model has an affiliation algorithm and whether its exit choice is predictive.
deviations: JuPedSim has no familiarity or affiliation state. Affiliation is represented by the journey weights of the occupants: 50/50 for the unfamiliar case and 20/80 (Exit 1 / Exit 2) for the affiliated case. The test verifies that exit choice follows the weights that the input assigns, not an affiliation model.
The scenario has two occupants at random positions in a 1.3 m by 1.0 m area around x = 5 m, instead of one occupant at a fixed position.

The pass rule is the suite's own: over 20 seeds (1 to 20), the Exit 1 and Exit 2 counts in the 50/50 case differ by no more than 10 % of the total, and Exit 2 is used more than Exit 1 in the 20/80 case. TN 1822 compares Exit 2 usage between the two scenarios and asks to repeat until it changes by no more than 1 %.
Occupants use the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m.

tests.title: Dynamic availability of exits
tests.definition: A room of 10 m by 15 m has two 1 m wide exits on the 15 m walls, equidistant from the bottom wall. One occupant without pre-evacuation time, walking at 1 m/s, stands in the room. Exit 1 becomes unavailable after 1 s of simulation time. The usage of both exits is checked. The test checks that the model can change the availability of routes over time, for example a door closed by smoke or heat.
tests.expected: The occupant does not use Exit 1. A model that cannot simulate dynamic exit availability should document that limitation.
deviations: Not run. The public interface of jupedsim-scenarios 0.7.3 cannot make an exit unavailable during a run: it removes exits only before a run. The test code writes the private agent state of the runner to send the occupant to Exit 2 at 1 s, so it would test the redirect that the test itself makes and not a response of the model to a closed exit.
The scenario file holds the room, both exits and one occupant with 50/50 journey weights. No time-dependent exit state is part of it.

tests.title: Congestion
tests.definition: A room of 8 m by 5 m is connected through a corridor 2 m wide and 12 m long to a stair that leads down, also 2 m wide (Fig. 12). The room holds 100 occupants, 2.5 persons/m2, with no pre-evacuation time and speeds that follow a population distribution. It is a modified version of IMO Test 11 with the stair going down. The test checks how the model produces congestion at a flow constraint.
tests.expected: Congestion forms at the exit of the room. It produces a steady flow in the corridor and congestion at the base of the stair, because the corridor and the stair have different flow characteristics. The evaluation is qualitative, by visual inspection if possible.
deviations: Stairs are not modelled. The corridor is a plain 2 m wide, 15 m long corridor that ends in the exit, with no stair or speed zone, so the congestion at the base of the stair is not tested. The corridor is 3 m longer than in Fig. 12.

The pass rule is the suite's own: the peak density in a window of 2 m by 0.5 m at the room exit (x = 3 to 5 m, y = 4.5 to 5 m) must exceed the peak density in a window of 2 m by 2 m in the corridor (x = 3 to 5 m, y = 15 to 17 m). The windows have different areas (1 m2 and 4 m2). The steady flow in the corridor is not measured.

The 100 occupants stand in a 7.4 m by 4.4 m area of the room, which is 3.1 persons/m2 locally and 2.5 persons/m2 over the 40 m2 room. Desired speeds are Gaussian with mean 1.2 m/s and standard deviation 0.2 m/s, and the body radius is the suite's default of 0.15 m.
The test runs one seed (42).

tests.title: Maximum flow rates
tests.definition: A room of 8 m by 5 m has a 1 m exit, centred on a 5 m wall. 100 occupants are placed in the room and assigned to the exit. The test is based on IMO Test 4. The test sets a conservative upper limit on the flow through the exit.
tests.expected: The flow at the exit over the whole period does not exceed a predefined maximum. TN 1822 gives 1.33 persons/m/s of IMO MSC/Circ.1238 as an example. A model that restricts door flows makes this a verification. A model with emergent flows makes it an external validation requirement. The tester documents the assumptions made for the flow, and for network models shows the sensitivity to the discretisation.
deviations: The restricted-flow reading is tested (decision D12): the jupedsim-scenarios exit throughput limiter is switched on at 1.33 persons/s, which is 1.33 persons/m/s for the 1 m exit, and the measured flow must not exceed it. This shows that the limiter enforces its cap. It does not show that the flow of the model without a limiter stays below the threshold.
The flow without the limiter is reported and not asserted, because the model alone produces a flow well above 1.33 persons/m/s.

The measured flow is (N - 1) / (t_last - t_first) / 1 m over the exit times of the 100 occupants. The pass rule is the suite's own: it must not exceed 1.33 persons/m/s by more than 1 %, an allowance for the 0.1 s trajectory sampling.
The 100 occupants stand in a 6.6 m by 4.6 m area of the room with the constant desired speed 1.2 m/s and the suite's default body radius of 0.15 m. The test runs one seed (42).

tests.title: Pre-evacuation time assignment
tests.definition: An 8 m by 5 m room has a 1 m exit. Ten occupants are placed at random positions in the room. A pre-evacuation time distribution (for example uniform, normal or log-normal) is imposed through the model's own input facility, and the run is repeated for every distribution family the model embeds. The test checks that each occupant starts to move at the assigned time. The tester chooses a statistical method that suits the distribution and repeats the scenario several times.
tests.expected: Each occupant starts moving at the appropriate time, and the pre-evacuation times of the whole population fall within the specified range. ISO sets no numeric tolerance.
deviations: The pass rule is the suite's own: the start times of 6 seeded runs (60 samples per case) are compared with 10 000 draws of the assigned distribution by a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test at alpha = 0.05. The start of movement is the first frame at which an agent has moved more than 0.05 m from its spawn point.

Three families are tested: uniform U(10, 100) s, normal N(60, 20) s and log-normal (mu = 4.586, sigma = 0.967). The scenario harness also embeds gamma and Weibull, which the suite does not test, although ISO asks for every embedded family.
The test compares the population with the distribution. It does not check each occupant's realised start time against that occupant's own assigned time.
Occupants walk at a constant 1.2 m/s. The exit is a 1 m wide, 0.3 m deep strip on the 5 m wall.

tests.title: Walking speed in a corridor
tests.definition: A corridor 2 m wide and 40 m long holds one occupant with an assigned walking speed of 1 m/s. The occupant walks the corridor and the covered distance is compared with the assigned speed. Models on a grid should repeat the test with the corridor rotated (for example 0 and 45 degrees) and consider cell-size sensitivity. The tester reports how the destination is set and whether agents accelerate to the assigned speed.
tests.expected: The occupant covers the corridor in 40 s. ISO gives no numeric tolerance; the comparison is the difference between expected and simulated result.
deviations: The corridor is 60 m long. The speed is measured over a 40 m segment (x = 10 m to 50 m), which excludes the start-up phase, instead of timing the whole corridor.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the mean transit speed over that segment is 1.0 m/s within 0.05 m/s.
Only the unrotated corridor is run. JuPedSim has no grid, so the rotation and cell-size checks do not apply, and the test does not record whether the agent accelerates.

tests.title: Walking speed on stairs
tests.definition: A stair 2 m wide and 10 m long, measured along the incline, is walked by one occupant with an assigned speed of 1 m/s, upwards or downwards. Models may use a speed factor or other input to change movement on stairs. The tester reports how the destination is set and documents how stair movement is represented.
tests.expected: The occupant covers the stair in 10 s, upwards or downwards. ISO gives no numeric tolerance.
deviations: The stair is a flat 10 m zone inside a 2 m wide, 30 m long corridor, with a speed factor of 0.5. The desired speed is 2.0 m/s, so the occupant crosses the zone at 1 m/s and takes 10 s, as ISO expects (decision D23). The test checks the speed-factor arithmetic, not a stair model.
The pass rule is the suite's own: the mean speed over the 10 m stair segment is 1.0 m/s within 0.05 m/s.
Up and down use the same flat zone, so the direction is not modelled and a single run stands for both. The effect of tread and width is not modelled.

tests.title: Movement around a corner
tests.definition: A 2 m wide L-shaped hallway has a 90 degree corner. Twenty occupants with no pre-evacuation time and a walking speed of 1 m/s start uniformly distributed in a 2 m by 4 m area at one end and walk around the corner. Figure 2 gives a horizontal leg of 10 m before the 2 m corner square and a vertical leg of 10 m. The test is a check of the available space, not of the shape of trajectories. The tester measures the flow entering and leaving the corner, records any change, and reports how the destination is set.
tests.expected: The occupants navigate the corner without penetrating the boundaries. ISO accepts a qualitative or a quantitative check of the paths.
deviations: Both legs are 2 m shorter than in Figure 2: the horizontal leg is 8 m before the 2 m corner square and the vertical leg 8 m above it.
The pass rule is the suite's own: all 20 agents evacuate and the centre of every agent stays at least its radius, less 1 mm, inside the walkable area (decision D16).
The flow entering and leaving the corner is not measured, and corners of other angles are not run.

tests.title: Assigned occupant demographics
tests.definition: A square room of 100 m by 100 m holds 100 occupants spread evenly. Walking speeds are assigned from a population chosen to match the expected building occupancy, and the data source is documented (ISO points to Lord et al., 2005, for example distributions). The test checks that the walking speeds the model produces agree with the assigned distribution, over several runs, with a statistical method chosen by the tester.
tests.expected: The simulated walking-speed distribution is consistent with the distribution specified in the scenario.
deviations: Desired speeds follow a Gaussian with mean 1.2 m/s and standard deviation 0.2 m/s. This is the suite's choice and is not tied to a published building population.
The scenario file has no exit. The test adds a full-width exit along the x = 100 m wall and measures each agent's median step speed while it walks the room.

The pass rule is the suite's own: over 3 seeded runs, the pooled mean and standard deviation of the measured speeds are each within 0.05 m/s of the assigned values, and the median of the per-run two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-values is above 0.05.
Agents are placed at random positions in the central 90 m by 90 m area, not on a regular grid.

tests.title: Horizontal counter-flows (rooms)
